He was neither a pest nor a pet, but something in between—a quiet presence that watched from the branches at twilight and vanished again before the stars came out.

The children of the village sometimes left offerings at the base of the tree—pieces of cheese wrapped in cloth, bits of dried meat, once even a silver thimble. Whether Eamon took the gifts or not was unknown; he never accepted anything openly, and yet, no offering ever remained untouched. The adults dismissed the offerings as childish fancy and told the children not to encourage the bird. But the children persisted, believing Eamon to be a kind of guardian, or perhaps a keeper of secrets.

Eamon never roosted among the other birds, never joined the raucous chorus of crows or the chatter of sparrows. He was aloof, and this made him both feared and admired. Some said he had once been a man, turned to bird by some old magic. Others whispered that he was the soul of a dead philosopher, still brooding over questions that had no answers. No one asked Eamon directly, of course—what owl would answer words spoken from below?

One evening, a young girl named Mira climbed the oak tree to sit beneath the hollow where Eamon made his nest. She brought with her a journal and a pencil, intending to write a letter to the owl, though she did not know what she would say. She waited for hours in the dimming light, sketching the shape of the tree, the way the wind moved through the branches, and the stillness of the hollow.

Eventually, Eamon appeared, perched on a branch just beyond her reach. He blinked once, then twice, his golden eyes unblinking and unreadable. Mira reached for her journal and began to write, not a letter, but something else entirely—a record of what she had witnessed, what she had felt, and what she suspected. As she wrote, the owl tilted his head, and for the first time, Mira thought she saw something like recognition in his gaze.

She did not know then that she had begun to unravel a mystery older than the village itself. Nor did she know that the owl, silent and watchful, had already chosen her as something more than just another admirer of the night.

For years, I believed the fault lay with me. That I alone misunderstood the rhythms of the world—how to read the air, when to step forward, or when to let the moment pass. It wasn’t until the day I missed the train that I began to suspect the world itself might be at fault.

I stood at the edge of the platform, arms folded, the collar of my coat turned up against the wind. The train would arrive in three minutes, according to the digital board that flickered like a dying star. But three minutes were never three minutes. I knew this. I had learned to count them in my head, to measure them by the number of advertisements that played and replayed behind the glass windows of the waiting area. And yet, when the train finally pulled into the station—late by eleven minutes, not counting the delay from yesterday—it passed me by without pause. I watched it disappear beyond the tracks, a great iron serpent swallowing itself in its own tail.

It was then, in the hush of sudden stillness, that I understood I had made a mistake not of timing, but of perception. I had assumed the train was waiting for me. I had assumed it knew I was there, that its presence was not random but intentional, that its arrival was a gesture, not a function of miles and minutes.

Since that morning, I’ve begun to notice similar patterns. The traffic light that turns green the second my foot lifts from the curb. The elevator that fills with people just as I reach its doors. Even the way the coffee shop barista, a quiet man with ink-stained hands and a habit of forgetting names, always places the wrong order on the counter at just the right moment. I used to chalk these things up to coincidence. Now I am not so sure.

What if we are all just spectators in a performance we do not understand? What if the world is watching us as closely as we watch it?

A part of me still believes it is absurd to think the universe is listening. Another part has started to wonder if it ever spoke at all—if the language it uses is not in words, but in the spaces between them. The silence after the train departs. The pause before the light changes. The way time stretches and contracts depending on how badly you want to catch something that is already moving faster than you.

And so I wait. On the platforms, in the intersections, beneath the flickering signs. I try to read the script of my life written in delays and detours, in the slow, deliberate pacing of the world pretending it is rushing.

But I have yet to find the first line.

The first thing I noticed was the smell—burnt wire and sea salt, with a dash of something sweet and artificial, like the kind of perfume you’d find in a discount bin at the edge of a mall parking lot. The second thing was the silence. Not the comfortable absence of sound that comes after a snowfall or the late-night hush of a sleeping city, but a silence that pressed into your ears like it was trying to communicate something you weren't built to understand.

We landed in a place that didn’t appear on any maps I owned, which was fine, because I only owned one map, a weather-worn thing that someone had stitched to the inside of a leather-bound field guide titled *Birds of the Western Hemisphere*. The stitching had come loose at the edges, and the continents curled in on themselves like pages drying in a library basement.

The others said it had been a mistake. That the navigation system had picked up interference from some abandoned radar station or a dead satellite. But I knew better. I’d seen this kind of thing before—places that refused to be found, that existed only in the margins between routes, where the GPS flickered and the compass spun like it had forgotten which way was north. I called these places "ghost stops," and I suspected there were hundreds of them scattered across the globe, waiting for someone to wander in.

We stepped off the old bus onto ground that was neither sand nor soil. It was gray and firm, with small nodules protruding like the knuckles of some ancient hand. No trees, no birds, no wind. Just the four of us and the drone of the engine cooling behind us.

Our guide, a wiry woman named Marla who claimed she’d crossed half the country in a truck that ran on recycled biodiesel and bad decisions, was already pulling a small notebook from her coat. She flipped to a page covered in neat columns of numbers and dates, then muttered under her breath, “Yep, definitely the same one.” She didn’t look surprised. She looked like she was confirming a suspicion she’d known all along.

“What’s the same one?” asked Leo, our quietest member, a college dropout with a habit of collecting old radio parts and reassembling them into things that didn’t quite work.

Marla glanced at me and smiled. “Ask me tomorrow,” she said. “Tomorrow might know the answer.”

And that, more than anything else, was what unsettled me most.

She always liked the hour before the tide came in. Not the moment when it arrived, surging and salt-thick, but the breath of silence before it, when the sand was still hard and the shorelines of driftwood and mussel shells had not yet been softened into a paste. It was the only time she ever allowed herself to walk slowly, to let her bare feet imprint the beach like footnotes in a book she had not yet read. The sand was cold here, even in summer, and it reminded her of something—something she had forgotten to remember. 

She had not planned on coming. Her husband had gone early to the market, and their daughter had stayed home with the neighbor to finish a homework assignment. The house sat quiet, and in that silence, she had packed a canvas tote with bottled water, a tattered copy of *The Tempest*, and a small knife she had taken without thinking. She walked to the beach not with intent but with resignation. 

Along the edge of the dunes, she found a patch of bleached wood, the ribs of a long-dead tree exposed like bones. She sat down, opened the book, and began to read. The wind picked at the pages, and the sky above was the kind of blue that makes you ache, that makes you want to hold something close and never let it go. She closed the book after a page, realizing she hadn’t understood a word. 

Instead, she watched a tern hover over the water, a white stitch in the air. It hovered and then dropped, straight into the sea, and came up empty. It hovered again. A second tern joined it. Then a third. They moved in concert, as if choreographed, though their movements held a kind of reckless precision. She thought of the old saying—that the birds knew where the fish were. Maybe, maybe not. She thought they looked hungry.

A group of boys on bicycles passed her in the distance, their laughter sharp as glass. She watched them until they were out of sight, and then she reached into the tote and pulled out the knife. She turned it over in her palm, smooth and weighty. She thought of all the things it could do, and none of them interested her. Instead, she laid it beside her on the sand.

She looked out to sea and wondered if anyone else felt it—the pull of something just beyond reach, the sense of a narrative already written, already finished, and still not understood. She thought of her daughter and hoped she was okay. She thought of her husband and how he never seemed to listen. She thought of the knife and how it had no answers either. 

The wind shifted. She stood. The tide was coming in now.

He checks the tide charts one final time before slipping the oars into the rowlock, the salt water catching the light and turning the blades to silver. The moon is nearly full, and the water is at its lowest, exposing the old stone wall that runs along the edge of the marsh like a broken spine. It’s the best time, he believes, to find them—those scattered remnants of the old world, buried beneath roots and silt and the slow work of erosion. 

The skiff slides into the channel, barely making a ripple. He rows with a steady rhythm, listening to the sound of the oar dipping and emerging, the soft creak of the wood, the whisper of the wind moving through the reeds. The marsh is quiet in the way it only gets to be at this hour, before the gulls have returned and the cranes stir in the fog. It is not empty, exactly, but it is waiting. 

A cormorant rises from the shallows ahead, black wings slapping the water as it gains altitude. He watches it disappear into the low-hanging clouds, then returns his gaze to the land. There, half-submerged in the mud, the rusted remains of a gate hinge. A few feet beyond, a bottle, green glass, etched with initials he can’t make out. He reaches down with gloved hands, careful not to sink into the soft ground, and lifts the relic into the boat. The water runs clean and cold through his gloves.

He rows on, past the old mill site, its foundation cracked and swallowed by the earth. The machinery long stripped, the river once turned by its wheels now lazy, indifferent. He imagines it running again, the wooden wheels groaning, the water churning, the scent of wet grain hanging in the air. But that world is gone. All of it. Even the memory of it fades with each passing season.

There is a bench on the far side of the channel, beneath the dead oak. He ties the skiff to a root and steps onto the land, boots sinking slightly into the soft ground. The bench is solid, carved with initials and dates from decades past. He sits, pulls a notebook from his coat pocket, and begins to sketch the bottle, the hinge, the outline of the wall beneath the water. 

It’s not treasure he’s after. Not money. It’s something else—something quieter, heavier. A record, maybe. A testament. A way to remember. 

He flips the page and writes the date. Then, beneath it, a name he can no longer place, but which feels important.

FOR years now, I have kept a careful record of the movements of the trolley on Third Street, especially during the hours between dusk and midnight. It was not, at first, a matter of interest but necessity. I had no car, no access to the subway, and the bus route had been suspended following the riots of ’92. The trolley, then, became both lifeline and curiosity. I began noticing patterns—how it sometimes skipped stops, how it seemed to pause longer at intersections where shadows deepened and alleys yawned open like old mouths. I began wondering: was the trolley running on schedule, or was it something else entirely?

The trolley’s bell is what first unsettled me. It rang not with the brisk, mechanical chime I expected, but with something more human—an almost mournful note, like a voice calling out into fog. And yet no one ever answered. I began arriving early, lingering at the corner where the streetlight blinked erratically, waiting for the ghost of a signal, the flicker of a conductor in the control room above.

The trolley itself is a relic. A single car, olive-green with rusted hinges and glass that never quite closes. Inside, the seats are torn, the ceiling tiles warped, and there is a smell of mildew and stale coffee. Still, it runs, and it runs reliably enough, though never on time. I’ve seen it stop at a cross street and wait for no one, doors open wide, as if expecting someone to materialize from the dark. Once, a man in a raincoat stepped on, glanced back at the empty sidewalk behind him, and whispered, “She’s not coming.” Then he sat in silence until we arrived at the next stop, where he vanished into the night as though he had never existed.

Passengers are few after ten. When they do come, they arrive like fragments of stories—the elderly woman who buys roses at the flower cart near the 7-Eleven and holds them cradled in her lap, the teenager with headphones who reads philosophy in the flickering light, the man who traces maps on the windows with his finger as though the glass were a portal. I have never spoken to any of them. Not once. It is easier to observe, to let the trolley do the talking for me.

Some nights, the trolley does not appear at all. In its absence, the street feels quieter—not empty, but absent of its usual rhythm. The air grows still, the streetlights hum faintly, and I begin to suspect that the trolley is not simply a vehicle, but something else entirely. A vessel. A carrier. Perhaps even a witness.

And I, a chronicler of its passage, a keeper of its silence, have begun to feel its pull—its need to be understood.

The fog has a green cast to it, thick and low, settling like a sheet over the estuary where the river forgets itself in the sea. On the narrow dock, he stands with binoculars at his eyes, watching for the terns to lift. Their flight patterns are erratic, looping, diving—almost playful—but to him they signal something more deliberate, a coded response to the unseen currents below. He has come here to wait.

The boat is moored beyond the pilings, bobbing gently, its hull a dull silver in the murk. A single lantern hangs from the bow, casting more shadow than light. The nameplate, if it ever existed, has long since rusted away. Inside the cabin, something hums—a refrigerator perhaps, or the ghost of a motor, or his own pulse. 

He checks the watch twice in a row. Thirteen minutes behind schedule. Not a problem, he thinks. Time bends here. He remembers her saying that once, her voice steady, certain, as if speaking from somewhere beyond the room. She had been reading from the naturalist, the one who claimed the earth was shaped by slow, invisible forces—layers of pressure, erosion, the turning of stones beneath ice. She had smiled then, or maybe he imagined it, the corners of her mouth lifting just slightly before she closed the book.

A gull caws in the distance. He pockets the binoculars and walks the length of the dock, careful not to step on the boards that groan. At the end, he stops. The water is not still. It moves with a quiet insistence, a rhythm he knows but cannot name. He kneels and touches the surface. It is colder than he expects, and for a moment the world narrows—just the wet, the breath, the sound of his name spoken once, long ago, in a kitchen lit by a single bulb.

There’s a crate at the base of the pilings. Weathered planks, a broken lock, a tarp half-flapping in the wind. He doesn’t open it. He never does. It’s not what’s inside that matters, but what it represents. Absence. Possibility. A held breath.

Back at the boat, he climbs aboard and lowers the hatch. The cabin smells of salt and mildew, of things stored too long and left to dream. He sets the binoculars on the bulkhead, adjusts the seat, and reaches for the throttle. The engine starts without complaint. He waits a moment, letting the vibrations settle in his chest, matching his heartbeat to the machine’s steady chug.

Then, slowly, he pushes off.

The launch of the Orion-class submersibles was heralded as the dawn of a new era in undersea exploration, a bold leap into the abyss where mystery clung to the walls of trenches deeper than the sky was wide. I remember the first time I saw one of them—sleek, metallic, and humming faintly with the kind of electricity that makes your skin prickle—its nose slicing through the black Pacific waters outside the naval yard at Pearl. It was supposed to be silent, they told us. A vessel of pure motion, a ghost in the sea. But silence, in the ocean, is a myth. Even the most advanced of machines hums, breathes, pulses like something alive.  

I had just transferred from the Arctic Reconnaissance Unit, where I’d spent two years studying ice floe displacement and tracking the migratory patterns of belugas using sonar arrays that more closely resembled cathedral bells than scientific instruments. Down here, in the warm Pacific, we were dealing with something else entirely—an ambition to reach the unseeable, to touch the bottom of the world where no flag had flown and no human had walked. The Orion was designed to do exactly that: descend to depths beyond the reach of conventional submarines, to map hydrothermal vents and study bioluminescent life forms in a darkness older than time.  

We were given a single training week aboard the vessel before deployment. The crew was small, handpicked. There were engineers, biologists, and navigators, all of us bound by a shared sense of the absurdity in what we were attempting. The captain, a retired marine geologist named Driscoll, carried himself with the stoicism of a man who had buried his share of failures in the sediment of the seafloor. He spoke little, but when he did, his words were clipped and precise, like orders from a machine.  

The first descent was scheduled for dawn. Before we slipped beneath the surface, Driscoll paused near the bridge, looking out at the horizon where the sky met the sea in a seam of silver. "We're not going to see the bottom," he said. "But we’ll feel it."  

And feel it we did. The pressure built like the hush before a scream. The Orions moved with a grace that seemed impossible for anything man-made, gliding through the dark like thoughts. And somewhere below us, in the cold, the unknown stirred.

There was a time when the telephone rang only during emergencies—funerals, fires, sudden departures—but now it sings with a kind of programmed insistence, as if calling were itself the emergency. It has become the most ordinary thing to answer and hear no voice, only a recording that promises connection and asks again, politely, perhaps with a touch of exhaustion, whether you are still there. Sometimes it plays a woman humming, a tuneless, looping hum that might once have meant someone was waiting for you, that someone had not yet hung up. But no, the silence was never silence anymore—only the breath of machines preparing themselves for speech.

I answer and listen to the hum most mornings, sipping lukewarm coffee, staring out at the overhanging trees that bend too close to the gutter. Their branches whisper against the window, a language older than words, speaking of decay and renewal, of things growing where they should not. I used to think the trees were watching me, but now I believe they are merely listening to the same hum on the other side of the glass.

I think often of the man who used to live next door, Mr. Ellery, who kept a parrot in a cage that hung from the porch railing. That bird could mimic any tone—laughter, coughs, the screech of a subway car. Once, late at night, I heard it scream my name, loud and distorted, and I woke in such a way that I did not know if I had dreamed it or if the bird had learned it from the hum of the machine. Mr. Ellery moved out the following spring, without a note or a goodbye. His neighbor left behind only the parrot, which flew one morning with a practiced squawk and never returned.

Now, the house is rented. I don’t know by whom, or what kind of silence has taken root inside those walls. The telephone keeps singing, and the trees press closer. I wonder if the new tenant hears the same hum. I wonder if anyone answers the phone anymore, or if we have all simply learned to let it play until the music stops, until the machines decide we’ve listened long enough.

He walked with the weight of the rifle in the crook of his arm, its stock still smelling of oil and sweat from yesterday's cleaning. The road ahead of him was gravel, broken and thin in places, and the dust had begun to settle into the morning air in faint ribbons, like smoke from a fire smothered too soon. Behind him, the town had already shut itself in sleep, curtains drawn tight, doors bolted, but the sky was wide open, washed pale with the coming of the sun. He had no idea how far the fox might have run, how far it might yet go.

The fox had been a problem for weeks—small at first, the odd missing hen, the scent of something wild drifting close to the coop before scattering into the hedges. But lately, the thefts had grown bold. Rabbits gone whole from their cages. Chicken feed scattered in the corners of the barn like confetti. And always the tracks—those clever, nimble prints, curling through the mud like ink spilled on the ground.

He didn’t blame the creature for wanting food. Not entirely. But it was the way it looked at him that had settled in his chest like a stone. When it had seen him last, crouched on the hillside with its back to the wind, the fox had paused. Its ears had twitched. Its tail had flicked once, slow and deliberate, like a question mark. And in that moment, he had known it was watching more than just for escape. It was watching for weakness.

He had taken to dreaming about it since. In the dreams, the fox wore his face. In the dreams, it ran through his fields not out of hunger, but purpose. It was returning something it had stolen, or demanding something it had taken. In the morning, he would wake with the taste of rust in his mouth and the feeling that he hadn’t slept at all.

Now, moving uphill, the rifle swayed slightly with each step, and the sun climbed higher, casting long shadows of the pine trees behind him. The air smelled of damp earth and the first green of spring, though spring had come late this year. Still, he kept walking. Because somewhere up ahead, just beyond the crest of the hill, the fox would be waiting. Or it wouldn’t. Either way, he was tired of the game. Tired of feeling like a man standing on the edge of a story he could not write. 

He stopped at the crest. Below, the valley spread out soft and green, broken only by the ribbon of the road and the distant glimmer of the river. Somewhere in that quiet patchwork, the fox had a plan. He hoped he had one, too.

The Director of the United States Postal Service was observed yesterday afternoon in a state of mild bewilderment, standing amidst a swarm of letter-carriers, none of whom were delivering mail. Instead, they had begun to wear their sacks as capes and were marching in slow, deliberate circles along Constitution Avenue. The press had dubbed the phenomenon “Operation Posture,” a nod both to the service’s acronym and the peculiar, rigid poise of the men and women who, rather than sorting letters, were striking poses with the grace of trained marionettes. 

The cause of this transformation was widely attributed to the recent installation of the Zeta-9 Sorting Engine, a machine so advanced it purportedly required no human intervention. Designed to interpret handwritten addresses with the precision of a scholar, it had instead developed a peculiar habit—every time a postmark was applied, the date shifted unpredictably. Packages addressed to October 12 suddenly arrived labeled “October 34.” Invitations to birthdays were returned stamped with the year 1927, and newspapers landed bearing headlines from the 18th century.  

To compound the confusion, the machine had begun appending cryptic annotations to each parcel. One woman in Nebraska received a box of cat food with a note reading, *For the feline historian of the 31st century.* Another man in Maine opened a letter from his nephew only to find the envelope sealed with wax and embossed with a sigil resembling an owl holding a candle in each wing.  

When questioned about the situation, the Postmaster General was quoted as saying, “We anticipated delays, yes, but not this. We’re looking at a breakdown not just of logistics, but of chronology itself.” Attempts to recalibrate the Zeta-9 had resulted in the machine producing postcards of cities that no longer existed and mailboxes that hummed softly with what sounded like lullabies from the future.  

Meanwhile, the carriers, perhaps inspired by the machine’s odd behavior, had entered into a state of collective performance art. They refused to speak, communicated via semaphore, and began composing poetry using only stamps and return labels. A letter addressed to the President was discovered with its contents entirely in iambic pentameter, written in invisible ink that revealed itself only when read aloud.  

No one could agree whether this was a malfunction, a metaphor, or a revolution in communication. But one thing was certain—the United States Postal Service was no longer just delivering messages. It was delivering time itself, folded neatly into envelopes, with a stamp, a seal, and a warning.

On the platform, a man in a moth-eaten navy blazer and a tie printed with tiny yellow birds stands perfectly still, his hands clasped behind his back. He is not looking at the train, nor at the tracks, but at a spot above the farthest tree line, where the sky begins to curl inward like the edge of a page in an old book. Behind him, a woman in a camel-hair coat folds and unfolds a crumpled flyer, repeating the motion like she might fold a flag into a pocket. The train that is supposed to arrive at 8:17 is running five minutes late, but neither of them moves.

The man adjusts his glasses, a small click of metal and plastic. He checks his watch. The numbers glow faintly. The numbers do not match the station clock. He glances at the woman again, who remains fixed in her rhythm. She wears a ring on her thumb, a thing of tarnished silver and a green stone. Her eyes are red-rimmed, not with sorrow exactly, but with something closer to sleeplessness—a kind of hollow alertness.

A child waddles by with a deflated balloon attached to a string wrapped around his wrist. The balloon flutters in a nonexistent breeze, catching bits of dust off the floor. He follows in the wake of his mother, who is talking on a phone. “I need another hour, yes,” she says. “If he misses this one, we’ll catch the next.” Her voice is smooth, practiced, as though this is not the first time today she’s arranged someone else’s schedule around her own.

The man in the blazer exhales sharply through his nose. It is not a sigh, not quite. He shifts his weight slightly, the creases in his trousers catching the light. He is tall, but he does not stand tall. He stands with the slight slouch of someone who once had a purpose and lost it somewhere behind a door that can't be opened again.

Nearby, a vending machine hums. Its glass is fogged, and through the distortion, candy bars and soda cans appear half-drowned in the gloom. The woman finally halts her folding, smooths the flyer with both palms, and reads it aloud under her breath. The words, if they meant anything, were lost in the static of the air. 

At precisely 8:20, the distant wail of the train’s horn cuts through the station like a blade. The man straightens. The woman pockets the flyer. The child drops the string, and the balloon drifts upward, caught by a sudden current. It disappears behind the ceiling tiles, swallowed whole. 

No one applauds. No one speaks. The man watches the trees again. The woman stares at the tracks. The train is coming.

The city was never meant for pigeons, but here they were—perched on the spines of statues, nesting in the eaves of abandoned libraries, circling the clock towers like thoughts the city refused to speak aloud. Once, people fed them. Now they left crumbs in the shape of complaints, folded letters addressed to no one in particular, tucked between gutter bars. The pigeons ate the words and grew fat on silence.

In the shadow of the old courthouse, now defunct and sold for parts, there lived a man named Eliot who believed pigeons were the last witnesses of truth. They saw everything, he told anyone who would listen, and remembered everything. “A pigeon,” he said, “can tell you the exact hour a mayor took the bribe, or when a lover’s heart turned to ash.” His neighbors thought he was mad. Or maybe they just thought he was tired. Eliot had once been a judge, now he judged birds.

He wore his robes indoors for warmth and dignity, though the house had no heat and the dignity had long since melted. On his desk sat a typewriter, yellowed and cracked, where he transcribed what the pigeons whispered to him. “They murmur in Latin,” he wrote in his notes. “Not because they’re learned, but because it’s the language of things that have already happened.”

Each morning, Eliot climbed onto his roof with a notebook and a handful of breadcrumbs. He’d feed the birds, then listen. Not with his ears—those had dulled years ago—but with the hollow space behind them, the part of him that had grown quiet enough to let the pigeons talk. He recorded their revelations in careful, looping script: *At 11:17 on Wednesday, the third bird from the left blinked twice. This indicates the mayor has lied three times already this week.*

His findings were published in a journal titled *Avian Verdict*, circulated only among the city’s more eccentric citizens. One such reader was Clara, the librarian, who kept a framed clipping near her desk. She never asked questions about the origins of the journal. She simply believed, or wanted to believe, that somewhere, someone was keeping the city honest.

One afternoon, a pigeon landed on her shoulder with something heavy in its beak. When she unwrapped the note, it read: *The fire under the bridge was set by the man with the missing button.* She showed it to the police, who laughed. They told her to find a hobby. She returned to the library, the note tucked safely in her coat pocket, and waited for the birds to speak again.

The man stood at the edge of the tarmac, a single suitcase at his feet, watching the plane taxi too slowly for comfort. The airport was small, the kind that smelled of kerosene and tired optimism, its fluorescent lights flickering over a handful of passengers who moved with the quiet urgency of people who’ve seen too many departures without return. The man in the tan trench coat waited. He didn’t check his watch, though he knew the time. He had learned not to count minutes.

Behind him, the terminal hummed with static conversation and the occasional burst of laughter that didn’t quite reach him. A child tugged at his mother’s hand, pointing to something on a screen. The man wondered if the child saw ghosts, or just saw.

He was not a stranger to disappearances. Not in the metaphorical sense, nor the bureaucratic kind, either. He had once walked into a border checkpoint and never walked back out. Not in person. Not in photograph. Not in memory, as far as anyone but him knew. He had paid to be erased, and then he had forgotten the price.

The suitcase at his feet was light. A couple of shirts, a book bound in imitation leather, a pack of chewing gum that would never be opened. Inside the false bottom, a passport with a name he had not spoken aloud in six months. He had chosen it for its rhythm—three syllables, one pause, a breath between letters. Easy to remember, hard to mispronounce.

The plane banked, wings carving a lazy arc across the sky. Clouds gathered in slow, deliberate rows. Somewhere beyond them, someone was already forgetting him. Or pretending to.

He lit a cigarette, the flame catching at the edges of his reflection in the window of the terminal. The man who stared back did not look like the man he used to be, and that was the point. He had shed skin like a snake, layer by layer, until nothing remained but bone and instinct. He had left behind cities and names, jobs and reasons. All he carried now were choices he had not yet made.

The gate attendant tapped him on the shoulder. Boarding time, he said, in the clipped tone of someone who had long since stopped believing in destinations. The man nodded. Exhaled. Stiffened the collar of his coat against the cold air that would soon fill the cabin.

As he walked toward the jet bridge, he glanced back once. The suitcase remained exactly where he had left it, untouched. A mistake, perhaps. A test. Or a final message from the man who had once existed before this one.

The train was late by an hour when Anjali arrived at the platform. The air in the station smelled of boiled lentils, diesel, and the faintest trace of jasmine oil someone had rubbed into their hair too close to their neck. She adjusted the strap of her satchel, which carried nothing but her passport and a single photograph folded carefully in a plastic sleeve, and checked the departure board again. Numbers changed. Letters rearranged themselves into different lies. 

Around her, the station pulsed with movement. Men in starched white uniforms swept the floors with brooms so long they might have once belonged to gods. A boy, no older than twelve, balanced a stack of teacups on his head and moved between groups of tourists with the precision of a surgeon avoiding blood. A woman in a saffron sari stood in a corner chanting something under her breath, her fingers moving through beads as if counting the seconds until a miracle.

Anjali had rehearsed this moment in her head, standing by the window of her hotel room in Jaipur, watching the sun sink behind the Aravallis. She would not cry. She would not look back. She would board the train and sit by the window and watch the world blur into memory. 

But when the conductor finally announced the delay, and the crowd surged forward with their tickets and their expectations, she faltered.

She had not expected the heat. Not in the station, where the ceiling fans circled lazily above the heads of passengers, nor in the waiting room, where the AC was broken and a sign read THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT IN THREE LANGUAGES. She had not expected the weight of all that she was leaving behind to settle itself in her throat like swallowed glass.

On the bench beside her sat a man in a faded suit, his face shaded by a newspaper. He had a crossword puzzle partially completed in blue ink, and a thermos clutched in his lap as if it were a child. Beside him, a young couple argued quietly, their hands fluttering like trapped birds. The boy pointed at the departure board. The girl shook her head. They did not speak in English.

Anjali pulled out her phone and typed a message. She read it twice, then deleted it. The words would not come. What was there to say?

The train arrived with a screech that startled the pigeons perched on the signal towers. The doors opened. And just like that, the world began to move again.

There is a man on the train platform who carries a typewriter in a brown leather case. He wears a rumpled suit, the collar of his undershirt peeking from beneath it like a small bird seeking shelter. He checks his watch every thirty seconds, but never glances at the departure board. Around him, the station hums with murmured conversations, the shuffle of briefcases and suitcases, the occasional cry of a child lost and quickly reunited. The man stands beside a pillar, his shadow stretching long and thin over the cracked tile.

He opens the typewriter case. Inside is no machine. Only a stack of pages, folded, sealed with a rubber stamp that reads *Not for Public Consumption.* The man touches the corner of the top sheet with reverence, as if brushing against the spine of a sleeping animal. He does not read them. He has read them many times. He is waiting.

Across the platform, a woman in a red coat moves slowly toward the tracks, her eyes fixed on the horizon where the rails disappear into fog. Her breath forms clouds, each one a tiny world of secrets. She carries no luggage, only a small silver flask in her coat pocket. The man sees her and stiffens. He closes the case gently, as though closing the lid on a coffin.

The woman pauses near a bench. A child has left an apple core behind. She picks it up, examines it for a moment, then drops it back to the ground, untouched. The man watches her. He remembers a woman with a red coat. Not this one, but one like her. Years ago, in another station, under different lights, with a different kind of silence.

A train arrives with a sigh. Doors open. Passengers pour out like ink from a pen. The man does not move. The woman in red begins to walk toward him, her steps slow, deliberate. She does not smile, but there is something tender in the angle of her shoulders. He steps back into the crowd. Not in fear, but in the old habit of retreat.

Somewhere nearby, a radio plays a song he once loved. It is playing in the background of everything now. He cannot remember the name of the song, or the artist. Only that it is a lullaby of sorts, for people who have forgotten how to dream.

The train departs with a hiss. The platform empties. The man and the woman stand alone, separated by meters, by meaning. The fog thickens. Something has shifted between them, though neither speaks. In the silence, the typewriter case rests at his feet, the pages inside waiting to be opened again.

Before the war, the bakery on Rue des Merveilles was known for two things: its sourdough, which had a bite sharp enough to wake the dead, and the old man who baked it, whose name no one could recall—though some claimed it was Pierre, others insisted it was Paul, and a few whispered that he wasn’t French at all but a forgotten soul from a colder, northern place. He didn’t speak to anyone, not really, only nodded and measured flour with the precision of a watchmaker. The regulars liked that. Mystery, they said, made the bread taste better.

After the war, the bakery was still there, but the old man was gone. In his place stood a young woman named Margot, who wore flour-dusted aprons too tight for her slight frame and who baked with the same quiet diligence, as though continuing a conversation he’d never finished. The sourdough remained, but the people had changed. The soldiers who once bought loaves by the dozen for ration boxes were replaced by mothers with tired eyes and children with sticky fingers. Still, the line outside the shop curled around the corner most mornings.

One spring morning, Margot opened early, the shutters creaking like a held breath. She moved through the routine with a grace that betrayed years of repetition: kindling the fire, feeding the oven, testing the dough beneath her palms. But when she reached for the starter jar, she paused. Something was off. The jar, once sealed with a tight twist of cloth, sat open. Inside, the starter had fermented beyond recognition—dark, glistening, and humming faintly like a tuning fork struck in a vacuum.

She stared at it for a long time, then slowly uncorked a small bottle from behind the counter. The label was faded, the ink smudged: *Pour Lui*. She hadn’t touched it in years—not since he’d left, not since the war had taken everything. But today, the air felt heavier, the silence louder. She poured a single drop into the bowl.

By midday, the bread smelled different. Not wrong. Not unfamiliar. Just… older. Warmer. Some customers noticed, though they couldn’t say how. Others only knew that for the first time in years, something in the world felt like it might be healing.

She had always imagined that the first time would be in the rain, beneath a bridge, or on the steps of a cathedral, where the world’s noise receded enough for a moment to feel sacred. But it wasn’t like that at all. It was midday, in the dusty kitchen of a rented house in Córdoba, and the sunlight fell through the blinds in stripes that looked like prison bars. She stood at the sink, her back to the window, and watched her breath fog the glass. Her name was Clara, or it was something close to that—names were slippery in the heat—and the man who touched her there was named Pablo, or was it Mateo? He had a name that meant something like "gift" or "warrior." She had forgotten.

Pablo, or Mateo, had arrived that morning with a sack of oranges and a story about a dead uncle and a key to a forgotten room. He said the house was hers now, or it would be, if she stayed. The house was warm with dust and memory. Every drawer was full of letters addressed to people who had long since moved away, or perhaps never existed at all. The walls were thin, and she often thought she heard laughter when there was no one there, though maybe that was just the wind.

She had spent the morning reading aloud to herself in the front parlor, the pages turning slowly beneath her fingers, and the words—written in a careful, looping hand—had taken on the quality of a chant. There was a rhythm to them, a soft insistence that pulled at something buried deep. She did not understand the language fully, but she understood enough to know it was not entirely false.

When Pablo came in, he found her curled on the couch, a book balanced on her knee, and he asked if she was hungry. She said no, though she was, and he prepared something from the oranges and whatever else he could find in the pantry. She watched him work, his movements precise, deliberate, and wondered how long it had been since someone else had fed her, truly fed her, with care and not just necessity.

The kitchen smelled of citrus and something else—something faint, like the scent of old linen or an unspoken apology. She closed her eyes and felt the air shift between them, as if the house itself had leaned in to listen.

THE NEW AGE OF POSTAL AVIATION HAS ARRIVED, OR AT LEAST THAT IS WHAT WE ARE TOLD BY THE HEADS OF OUR NATION’S MAJOR MAIL DELIVERY SYSTEMS, MEN WHO WORE TIEFLINES WITH THE STIFFNESS OF MORAL PURPOSE AND EYES THAT GLISTENED WITH THE KIND OF RESOLUTE HOPE USUALLY ASSOCIATED WITH MEN WHO ARE EITHER VERY RICH OR VERY STRANGE. According to these men, the future of delivery is airborne, and nothing is more emblematic of this new era than the sleek and silent PostJet-3X, a machine so advanced it supposedly requires only one pilot, two automated navigators, and a single paralegal to interpret the ever-growing web of regulations governing high-altitude postage.

The PostJet-3X does not merely deliver mail; it transcends the boundaries of traditional conveyance, soaring above highways and bypassing the limitations of gravity with the kind of indifference usually reserved for metaphysical dilemmas. It is said to carry letters, packages, and even perishables—though no one has yet been able to confirm whether the perishables remain edible upon arrival, which, given the current state of food science and the recent scandal involving the “Expresso Express” incident, remains a matter of deep public concern.

Before the advent of the PostJet-3X, the United States Postal Service was a lumbering giant, its operations mired in red tape, rusted trucks, and the occasional postal worker who, legend insists, once delivered a letter to the wrong house and then lived in it indefinitely, pretending to be the owner. There were also problems with delays, weather, and the occasional postal eagle—a relic of an earlier era when birds of prey were trained to drop letters through open windows, a method now deemed inefficient, unsanitary, and vaguely fascist.

But no more. The age of the pigeon is over, and the era of the jet is here. According to the Department of Aeronautical Correspondence, the PostJet-3X has reduced average delivery times by 83.7%, increased accuracy by 120.4%, and significantly lowered the number of complaints from citizens about missing birthday cards and incorrect utility bills. Still, skeptics remain.

Among them is PostMaster General Horace Wren, a man of quiet demeanor and a voice that sounds like a typewriter trying to apologize for a mistake. Wren argues that the PostJet-3X, for all its technological splendor, is a hollow shell of the postal service’s former soul, which, he claims, lay not in speed but in the ritual of the handwritten note, the ink-stained thumbprint, and the slow, deliberate passage of time that only a paper envelope could contain.

Wren says nothing more. He merely watches the sky, where a distant glint reflects the future, and wonders if anyone is watching it for the right reason.

It happened during the off-season, when the arena was a ghost of itself, the echoes of sneakers squeaking long silenced. The custodian found it in the east wing, just beyond the old locker room, where the pipes groaned and the ceiling sagged under the weight of decades. There it lay, half-buried in a pile of rusted weights and moth-eaten jerseys: a leather basketball, cracked and dry, the name *J. Marlow* stitched in fraying cursive across the side.  

J. Marlow hadn’t played since ’72, when the league folded under its own bad debts and worse publicity. Some said he’d quit the night a referee tossed a ball at his head and said, *“Maybe this’ll teach you to smile, Mr. Hall of Shame.”* Others claimed it was the night he lost his daughter to meningitis, though no one believed a man who once laughed at death would let sentimentality get the better of him.  

Still, he left. Quietly. Without ceremony.  

The ball, though—it remained. Like a relic.  

The custodian dusted it off with the sleeve of his jumpsuit, and for a heartbeat, he swore it looked more like a man’s face than a piece of rubber and thread. The stitching seemed to twitch. He let out a nervous laugh and dropped it back into the pile.  

But J. Marlow had been back once before.  

Just a week prior, security cameras caught a figure wandering the concourse after hours. No badge, no flashlight, just a worn-out suit and the smell of bourbon clinging to his collar. They found him in the old press box, staring at a row of empty seats, one hand gripping a bottle like it was a baton for something unfinished. He didn’t say a word. Didn’t move. Didn’t blink. They let him be.  

And now this ball—this ghost in a ghost city—was the only thing left of the man who once made the court tremble.  

There was a time when J. Marlow could make a crowd forget the score, forget the odds, forget everything but the rhythm of the game. He played as if the world outside didn’t exist, as if the silence between dribbles and baskets was where the real magic lived. He wasn’t the fastest or the tallest, but he was the one they remembered.  

Now, the only thing left to remember him by was a ball that should have been buried with the league.  

Somewhere in the dark, the pipes gave a wet cough. The custodian turned off the light and locked the door behind him.  

No one noticed the ball roll slightly, just a fraction, as if something inside it still wanted to move, still wanted to play.

There is a man standing in the shadow of the marina, watching the tide recede. His face is weathered, sunbaked, like the wood of the dock beneath his boots. The salt air hangs thick with the scent of diesel and kelp, and somewhere beyond the chain-link fence, a gull cries — sharp, lonely, and too loud for the stillness.  

A dinghy rocks gently beside the moored boats, its hull cracked along the gunwales. A single oar lies across the stern. The man reaches into his coat and pulls out a folded map, the edges frayed, the ink faded. He unfolds it with care, smoothing it against the planks, and marks something with the tip of a knife. The blade catches the light briefly, then is gone again.  

Across the bay, a lighthouse swings its beam like a pendulum, sweeping through the dark. It misses him each time. He waits.  

On the far end of the dock, a boy no older than twelve is tying knots in a length of frayed rope. His hands are quick and practiced. He doesn’t look up as the man approaches.  

“You know what this is?” the man asks, holding out the map.  

The boy glances at it, then back to his rope. “Looks like a plan,” he says.  

The man grunts. “It is. But plans don’t mean much without a boat.”  

The boy nods. “You need help?”  

The man studies him for a moment. The boy’s face is clean-shaven, pale, as if he hasn’t been out in the sun enough. But his eyes are old. They don’t blink.  

“You ever row in those waters?” the man asks.  

“Once.”  

“That close to the rocks?”  

The boy shrugs. “Close enough.”  

The man nods again, more to himself. He folds the map, tucks it back into his coat. From his pocket he pulls a small glass vial filled with something dark. He holds it up to the fading light. The liquid swirls inside.  

“What is it?” the boy asks.  

“A memory,” the man says.  

The boy says nothing. The gull cries again. The tide continues to pull the bay into itself. Somewhere, a distant foghorn rumbles. The man watches it rise and fall like a breath.  

Then he turns, and walks away from the water, leaving the boy and the tide, the boat, the ropes, and the silence behind him.

The old man sat in the armchair with the back broken off, staring across the pasture where the fence once ran. The chair was positioned exactly where the gate had stood. He had moved the chair there three months ago, on the anniversary of the first time he’d locked it. The pasture was empty now, save for the cows, which kept their distance, as if aware they were not supposed to be in this part of the world anymore.  

He wore the same plaid shirt every day, even in the heat, even in the rain, the fabric faded to the color of memory. On his lap rested the ledger, covered in dust and the names of people who no longer came. The first entry was dated 1942. The last one, four years ago, was crossed out with a thick black line, the ink still fresh. He hadn’t written anything since.  

Every morning, without fail, he waited for the truck. The truck never came. Not since the man in the green hat stopped showing up. The man in the green hat had always left a bottle of something strong. Whiskey? Rum? Sometimes it was empty. Sometimes it wasn’t. The old man never opened it, just sat with it beside him, like a message.  

The birds had learned not to call too early. They stayed silent until the sun was high enough to cast the shadows of the trees in straight lines. Then they came. Then the crickets joined in. Then the pasture sang.  

He had trained the cows not to moo after the storm in August. The storm had broken the barn. The cows had wandered. They had eaten the scarecrow. He hadn’t rebuilt the barn. He hadn’t built a new scarecrow. The birds came anyway.  

His son had left home in '83. The old man remembered the date because it was the day the last cow died. He had buried the cow in the pasture. He had not buried his son. The son had written once, in a letter that smelled like smoke and salt. It read: *I hope you don’t miss me. I don’t miss you. I am fine.* The old man had read it aloud, over the cows, before folding it carefully and placing it in the broken drawer of the kitchen table.  

When the wind changed direction, he could smell the lake. It was not close, but the scent reached him in waves, as though the water remembered how to move. He would close his eyes and imagine it—water lapping, children screaming, the air tasting of lemonade and burnt toast. Then the wind would turn, and the pasture would smell like wet hay and rot.  

He counted the birds. Then he counted them again. They numbered eleven. Eleven was enough. More than enough.  

The sky turned gray. He looked up. The clouds were moving in the way the cows once moved, slow and thoughtful, like they owned the horizon.  

The old man waited. He had learned to wait.  

He had learned everything from the cows.

The train had been late twice already when Clara finally gave up waiting and settled onto the bench by the window, her notebook balanced across her knees like a shield. Outside, the dusk was thick with fog that clung to the tracks and blurred the hazy shapes of trees and distant streetlights. The air smelled of wet metal and someone’s stale perfume. She scribbled in the margins—*what you are afraid of, what you’re running toward, the difference between them*—then stared at the page and crossed it all out. Her pen tapped the leather cover until she remembered why she carried it: distraction, mostly, and to feel like a character in her own life.

Across from her, a boy in a red scarf read *Moby-Dick*. He flipped the pages with the kind of reverence reserved for holy texts, and every now and then he would pause, chew the inside of his cheek, and stare out the window as if the sea might appear just beyond the fog. Clara wondered whether he was reading to understand the book or if it was just the weight of it that mattered—how it anchored him. She envied that.

The train lurched forward with a groan, and the lights above their heads blinked on, casting a sickly yellow glow. Someone in the corridor began humming a tune too bright for the hour. It was the kind of melody that belonged to a sunny day and an empty room, and it didn’t fit the train’s rhythm. Still, Clara leaned closer to the window, as if the fog might part and reveal something meaningful, something not yet lost or forgotten. She thought of her mother, who used to say that meaning was just a word people used when they were tired of not understanding.

Her notebook lay closed now. She traced the grain of the leather with her thumb and tried to remember the last time she’d believed in beginnings. The train moved, slowly, steadily, toward wherever it was going, and Clara waited for the next page to turn.

On the evening the mayor declared the city’s first-ever holiday in honor of the forgotten sports, I sat in my kitchen staring at a bowl of lukewarm lentil soup and wondering whether I’d ever again feel the thrill of a perfectly timed steal in a half-court game played under flickering streetlamps. Back when we called the courts “The Halls,” and the net was more of a suggestion than a requirement, every bounce of the ball felt like a heartbeat, each missed shot a whispered prophecy.

But the city had cleaned things up. Now, every court was numbered, painted in fresh lines, and patrolled by security drones to prevent vandalism, which I suppose is a kind of respect, even if it’s cold and impersonal. I haven’t played in years—not really. I still go sometimes, just to watch the kids. They wear shoes that hover slightly above the ground, and their passes are sharp, sterile things. No sweat, no friction, no dust kicked up between toe-dragged halts.

I used to coach a team in the basement of the old hardware store. We played on wooden planks salvaged from the docks, the boards groaning with every pivot, every sprint backward to defend a three-pointer. The walls were covered in maps of imaginary leagues, names of players who would’ve been legends if only anyone had written down their scores. I once trained a boy named Eli who could shoot with one eye closed, and still miss. He was my favorite failure.

The new holiday, I learned, would feature tributes to the sports that time forgot—like the Great Midday Race, the sport of Thistle Kick, and of course, the ancient and sacred Ritual of the Floating Net. They’re even restoring the old Hall of Unplayable Events, a crumbling brick structure that once housed games so obscure and strange they had to be judged blindfolded. I was invited to speak. They said I had "authenticity." I didn’t ask what that meant.

So here I was, in my kitchen, waiting for the soup to cool, thinking about the last time I held a basketball in my hands. It felt heavier then, like it remembered me. The kids today say the old games were chaotic. I say they were alive.

The first time I saw the old man walk into the bar, he was leaning on a cane made from a baseball bat, its surface still etched with the grooves and scars of some long-forgotten game. He wasn’t asking for anything, just standing in the corner near the dartboard, watching the television where a basketball game buzzed with too much sound and too little meaning. The regulars barely noticed him. They were used to strangers—especially in a town this small, where every outsider was either a ghost or a ghost pretending to be alive.

His name, I later learned, was Walter, though I suppose I’m just as likely to have made that up. What I do remember is that he had the eyes of someone who had once seen something truly remarkable and had never quite stopped believing it was still out there, waiting to be found again. He wore a tan windbreaker, the kind that looked like it had been stitched together from pieces of older jackets, and underneath he had a t-shirt with a faded logo of a team that no longer existed. No one asked him about it. Around here, questions were only for people who didn’t know when to leave.

Walter came in nearly every day after that, always at the same time—just after lunch, when the sunlight through the window made the dust particles in the air seem like constellations. He never ordered the same drink twice, but he never really drank either. Instead, he talked. Not about the game, not in any real sense. He talked about the silence between the plays, the weight of the ball before the throw, the way the court used to feel like a living thing beneath your feet.

One afternoon, he told a story about a game he’d watched as a boy—how the crowd had gone so completely silent that even the sound of the clock ticking on the wall seemed to vanish. “That’s how it used to be,” he said, his voice low, almost to himself. “No noise, no lights, no nonsense. Just the game. And the people watching it like they were part of it.”

None of us said much after that. Some of us just kept looking at the TV, where the announcers barked over every missed shot like they were calling the end of the world. Others looked at Walter, who sat perfectly still, as though he was already somewhere else entirely.

A satellite is tumbling. Its solar panels catch the sun once every twelve minutes, each flash a brief and clinical punctuation mark in the silent void. It was designed to observe, not to drift. Designed to collect data on the migration patterns of the least tern, a bird that nests in dunes and flies in wide arcs across the southern coasts of the United States. The satellite is now a ghost circling for no reason, sending corrupted packets that resemble, in form only, the telemetry of birds learning how to return home. 

On Earth, in a glass-walled office overlooking a golf course where no one plays anymore, Dr. Elise Moreau stares at a screen that flickers with unreadable numbers. Her fingers hover over the keyboard. She is not a field biologist. She is a systems architect, a person who believes that the world can be predicted if you model it carefully enough. She has spent ten years building the software that interprets this satellite’s data. Now it cannot interpret anything. 

The least tern is supposed to be resilient. It is supposed to find its way back to old nesting grounds even after storms, droughts, coastal erosion. It is supposed to know what to do when the sand shifts beneath it. But the satellite suggests otherwise. The latest readings show a deviation. A large one. The terns are not returning to the barrier islands. Some are going inland. Others vanish entirely. The system Dr. Moreau built cannot account for these deviations. It assumes repetition, not rupture.

Outside, wind moves through the dry grasses near the fairway. A gull circles once, then again, before landing in the rough. It is not a least tern. Dr. Moreau leans forward, adjusting her glasses. She clicks on a file labeled *Last Known Coordinates – Tern Nesting Site, Texas Coast*. The map loads, a patchwork of green and beige. The satellite image is grainy, taken weeks ago, and already irrelevant. The terns have moved on—or left for good. 

She closes the program. For the first time in ten years, she does not know what to predict.

THE MODERN MANUFACTURE OF SADNESS IN THE INDUSTRIAL AGE began with a single realization: that sorrow is best when engineered. Not the raw, undiluted grief of ancient forests or forgotten names carved in stone, but sorrow as commodity, sorrow as brand, sorrow as carefully calibrated emotion with a shelf life and a customer satisfaction survey tacked neatly beneath it. Today, the factories bloom in clusters outside urban centers, their smokestacks exhaling not soot but something subtler—a vapor of melancholy, processed and sold by the ton.

Inside these plants, workers in starched blue uniforms move with mechanical precision, assembling kits of sadness. Each workstation is devoted to a specific component. At bench number 42, employees insert the element of loss: a single sheet of paper, folded once, inked with a name and date, then sealed inside a cardboard box labeled “What Was.” Down the aisle, another crew stitches together the narrative thread—printed scripts of regret, heartbreak, longing—all in the passive voice for maximum universality.

Quality control is rigorous. Machines hum with the soft whir of memory, testing each batch for emotional potency. If a package of despair falls below threshold levels (as happened last Tuesday with the lot of 7B-9X), it is rejected, ground into pulp, and recycled as filler in the next batch of generic nostalgia.

There is a science to it now. Psychologists, once skeptics of the entire enterprise, have since joined the board of directors. They assure the public that manufactured sadness is not only safe—it’s therapeutic. “It allows consumers,” they say in corporate press releases, “to experience catharsis in a controlled environment.”

Outside the factory gates, the town has grown quiet. The children walk home early, clutching their weekly dose of mild melancholy purchased at the corner store. Adults meet in parks to exchange stories of simulated heartbreak, each more poignant than the last, each carefully produced to feel authentic.

No one questions it much. After all, what is the alternative? The old kind of sadness—the spontaneous, unpredictable kind that arrived without warning, like a cold wind in August—is considered archaic, even dangerous. It lacks certification. It cannot be measured, bottled, or returned for a full refund.

Still, there are whispers. In the deepest corners of the factory, behind the locked doors of the R&D wing, one senior engineer has begun experimenting. He believes there is value in the old grief, in the kind that makes your hands tremble and your voice crack. He keeps a small vial of it hidden in a drawer, labeled simply “Uncurated.”

But the machines continue to hum. And the workers continue to stitch.

I DO NOT believe in ghosts, though I once believed in something close to them, or rather, I believed in the idea that people can carry the weight of the dead in their pockets like loose change. This is not a belief in the supernatural, exactly, but in the persistence of presence—the way certain voices echo in stairwells long after the speaker has vanished. I used to think that if you listened hard enough, if you sat perfectly still with your ear pressed to the world like a tuning fork, you might catch the faintest hum of those who came before you, their regrets stitched into the air like forgotten thread.

It began when my grandfather died. He was a man of few words and fewer gestures, a retired typesetter who spent his last years rearranging letters on index cards to form anagrams of names no one remembered. I used to find him in the kitchen with his hearing aid turned down low, muttering to himself in a language only he understood. When he was gone, I felt it not as absence but as subtraction—as though someone had taken a blade to the edges of the world, smoothing out the rough corners he’d left behind. And yet, in the weeks that followed, I started to hear him again—not in words, but in silences. In the creak of the old floorboards beneath the kitchen table. In the way the light bent when the afternoon sun hit the window just so.

I began to collect objects associated with him: a rusted paper clip he left on the windowsill, a spoon from the drawer he kept his coins in, a button missing from his winter coat. I arranged them on my desk like offerings or relics, trying to summon something back from the nothing he left behind. Sometimes I spoke to them. Sometimes I didn’t. I told myself it wasn’t superstition—it was memory, distilled into matter. That by keeping a piece of him in my space, I was keeping him alive in mine.

But then I realized something strange: the deeper I buried myself in this quiet ritual, the more I felt someone else watching me do it. Not my grandfather, necessarily, but another eye, another breath, lingering just beyond the edge of my awareness. It was the first time I considered the possibility that the dead might not simply haunt places—but people. That we are all, in some quiet way, haunted by the ones who taught us how to live—and how to miss.

The Ministry of Recreational Harmony has issued a new directive regarding the allocation of laughter quotas for citizen engagement during the Spring Festival. Each household must log a minimum of twelve genuine expressions of joy per member, recorded via the JoyMeter 3000, synchronized automatically with municipal sentiment servers.  

For the Lin family, this has proven challenging. Mrs. Lin, a retired taxonomist, finds mirth elusive since the relocation of the city’s botanical gardens. Mr. Lin, a former tailor turned community coordinator, has resorted to distributing novelty kazoos in exchange for documented glee. Their daughter, Xiaoling, now a remote worker in the Department of Virtual Tranquility, communicates only through curated emojis and algorithmically generated haiku.  

Last week, Xiaoling sent a transmission titled *Moss on the Porcelain Wall*. It read, *Cold rain falls slow like silk/ The wall breathes quiet green/ No laugh is born here.* The household sat in silence after receiving it. No one dared to comment on how moss, according to the Ministry’s recent Cultural Sentimental Edicts, is a symbol of national melancholia and must be eradicated in favor of structured floral arrangements.  

At precisely 9:00 AM, the JoyMonitor chimed. A voice, warm but clinical, intoned, “Please initiate your daily mirth activity.” Mr. Lin tapped his wristband and selected “Collective Laughter Exercise #7: Simulated Surprise at Unannounced Gifts.” He handed Xiaoling a wrapped box labeled *Mystery Object, Grade 3 Delight Inducer*. She opened it carefully and held up a rubber chicken.  

Mrs. Lin stared at it. “It is... yellow.”  

Mr. Lin nodded. “Yes. Very yellow.”  

Xiaoling tilted her head and, for a moment, there was a flicker across her eyes—something close to amusement. But it vanished quickly.  

“Recorded joy levels at 14%,” the monitor announced. “Target unmet.”  

The family exchanged glances. No one moved. Outside, the sky had taken on a dull gray hue. The JoyMonitor beeped again.  

“It’s a rubber chicken, Mom,” Xiaoling said finally, her tone flat but not unkind.  

“A chicken,” Mrs. Lin murmured. “With no feathers, no beak, only rubber. What is it doing here?”  

Mr. Lin sighed. “It’s for joy.”  

“For joy?” she repeated. “What kind of joy?”  

Xiaoling looked down. “The kind the government approves.”  

The JoyMonitor beeped once more. Then twice.  

No one laughed. But the moss behind them continued to grow, slow and silent, as if listening.

The general assembly of the Great Northern Ducks convened annually in the town of Frogleap, a place once celebrated for its annual amphibian migration but now remembered mostly for its fog and the solemn waddle of its feathered dignitaries. The conference took place in a converted warehouse, its walls papered with old maps and outdated diagrams of wetland drainage systems. Attendees, identifiable by their oil-slick sheen and webbed badges pinned crookedly to their vests, gathered in a semi-circle around a podium that had once been a shipping crate reinforced with nails. 

This year’s president of the ducks was a particularly portly specimen named Waddlemere, notable not only for his size but for his uncanny ability to speak in full paragraphs using only quacks and the occasional honk. He had prepared a lengthy address on the importance of preserving migratory routes, the necessity of clean water, and the dangers of human encroachment. But before he could begin, a young drake, barely out of adolescence, burst into the hall flapping wildly, his feathers soaked through from a recent skirmish with a garden gnome. “They’re coming!” he cried, or rather, a sound resembling that, and then collapsed into a puddle at the base of the crate podium.

Waddlemere, undeterred, quacked authoritatively and adjusted the binoculars tied around his neck—tied there, in fact, because he refused to let them fall into the lake again. The room fell silent, the murmurs of the gathering quacking subsiding into the kind of quiet only achieved when a duck realizes it might be missing something important. “Honk,” Waddlemere intoned, “what you bring is… troubling.”

The young drake nodded, his bill still dripping. “Honk. Quack-quack honk!”

A hush spread through the assembly. The meaning was clear: the humans were building again. Not just any buildings, either—pond-free zones. Dry, brick, sterile places with no moss, no algae, and worst of all, no mosquitoes.

The crowd erupted into a cacophony of protest. Some flapped their wings in agitation. Others began to preen nervously, though few believed that a bit of neatening would convince the builders otherwise. Waddlemere raised a wing for silence. “Honk-quack,” he said, “we will not be driven from our waters. We shall adapt. We shall innovate.” He paused, then added, with the solemnity of one who had once nearly drowned in a birdbath, “We shall… float forward.”

And so, the Great Northern Ducks voted unanimously to form a coalition for the preservation of wetlands—legally, diplomatically, and, if necessary, artistically. After all, what better way to save a pond than to turn it into a stage for duck opera?

Golf was once played by torchlight. Not in the manner of a romantic twilight foursome, but in literal darkness, with flickering flames casting shadows over the greens and hazards. Back when the game had not yet been sanitized—before floodlights and manicured fairways—the elite of [REDACTED] took to playing in moonlit fields or candlelit halls. I remember hearing these tales whispered among the staff at the Country Club, the very place where such traditions had died, buried beneath layers of bureaucracy, insurance, and a growing aversion to risk. These stories were not meant to be told with pride, but they lingered in the corners like forgotten ghosts, waiting for someone bold enough to speak their names.

I grew up in [REDACTED], the son of a groundskeeper, a man who spoke of the old course as if it were a cathedral. He never played, not really—he maintained it, tended to its scars and silences. He told me once that the original 18th green was nothing but a clearing in the woods, lit by kerosene lamps until the storm of ’58 swept them all into the creek. Afterward, the course was modified to meet modern standards. The trees were trimmed. The paths widened. The hazards filled in. All the wildness was excised. “They wanted control,” he said, as he always did, shrugging as if it were a small thing, a slight to nature. But I knew, even as a boy, that he resented it. He resented the way the club turned tradition into regulation, the way they replaced the wind with sprinklers, the thrill of uncertainty with numbered bunkers.

As an adult, I returned for the first time in twenty years. The place looked like a museum now—polished, pristine, and utterly sterile. I walked the course with no clubs, just a notebook and a pen, mapping what I could remember of the original layout. There were subtle clues—the bend of the fifth fairway that once hugged a stream now paved for golf carts, the slight hump of the seventh green where a fox once made its den. I found a single lamp post near the 12th hole, its iron frame rusted and cracked. It had long since stopped functioning, but something about it hummed, as if waiting for the old magic to return.

I stayed for a week, sleeping in the maintenance lodge my father once occupied. Every evening I walked the course in silence, imagining the echoes of boots on soil, of laughter in the dark, of clubs striking balls with a sharp, defiant crack. I wondered if the game was ever truly meant to be seen at all.
